sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Bodyweight Pull Up is a fundamental compound upper body exercise that targets the latissimus dorsi, biceps, and upper back muscles.

Performed by hanging from a bar and pulling your body upward until the chin clears the bar, it is one of the most effective bodyweight exercises for building back width and upper body pulling strength.

Pull-ups require no equipment other than a bar and are a benchmark for relative body strength.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds a wide, V-tapered back
- Develops grip strength and forearm endurance
- Engages multiple muscle groups simultaneously
- Requires minimal equipment
- Improves posture and shoulder health
- Excellent indicator of relative body strength
- Easily scalable with bands or added weight
- Carries over to climbing, sports, and daily pulling tasks

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Latissimus Dorsi, Teres Major

Secondary: Biceps Brachii, Brachialis, Brachioradialis, Rhomboids, Lower Trapezius, Rear Deltoids, Core Stabilizers

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Hang from a pull-up bar with your palms facing away from you (overhand/pronated grip).
2. Hands should be slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
3. Arms fully extended, shoulders engaged (not shrugging up to ears).
4. Legs straight or slightly crossed behind you.
5. Core braced and body in a straight line.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Engage your shoulder blades by pulling them down and back.
2. Drive your elbows down toward your hips as you pull your body upward.
3. Continue pulling until your chin clears the bar.
4. Squeeze your lats at the top of the movement.
5. Lower your body back down in a controlled manner to full arm extension.
6. Avoid swinging or using momentum — maintain a strict form.
7. Repeat for the desired number of reps.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Using momentum or kipping to get over the bar
- Not achieving full range of motion (partial reps)
- Shrugging shoulders up to the ears instead of engaging lats
- Flaring elbows out instead of driving them down
- Not fully extending arms at the bottom
- Crossing legs and swinging to generate momentum
- Gripping too narrow or too wide
- Rushing through reps without control
- Craning the neck to get chin over the bar

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Pull-Up Bar (doorway, wall-mounted, or free-standing)
- Optional: Resistance Band (for assisted pull-ups)
- Optional: Weight Belt or Dumbbell between feet (for weighted pull-ups)
- Optional: Chalk (for improved grip)
- Optional: Gymnastics grips or gloves

sections.heading: Bar Setup
sections.content:
1. Ensure the pull-up bar is securely mounted and can support your body weight.
2. The bar should be high enough that you can hang with arms fully extended without your feet touching the ground.
3. If using a doorway bar, verify it is properly secured before each use.
4. For assisted pull-ups, loop a resistance band over the bar and place one foot or knee in the band.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Grip: Overhand (pronated), slightly wider than shoulder-width.
2. Arms: Fully extended at the start — dead hang position.
3. Shoulders: Pulled down away from ears, engaged and packed.
4. Core: Braced throughout the movement.
5. Legs: Straight or slightly bent, crossed if preferred.
6. Head: Neutral position, looking straight ahead.
7. Breathing: Exhale on the way up, inhale on the way down.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Chin-Ups (underhand grip): More biceps involvement
- Lat Pulldown: Machine-based alternative, adjustable resistance
- Neutral Grip Pull-Up: Palms facing each other, easier on wrists
- Inverted Row: Bodyweight pulling at an angle
- Band-Assisted Pull-Up: Reduced bodyweight for beginners
- Machine-Assisted Pull-Up: Counterweight to reduce difficulty

sections.heading: Pull-Up Variations
sections.content:
Standard Pull-Up: Classic overhand grip, shoulder-width or wider
Wide-Grip Pull-Up: Greater lat stretch and width emphasis
Close-Grip Pull-Up: More biceps and lower lat engagement
Weighted Pull-Up: Added resistance via belt or dumbbell
Slow Negative Pull-Up: Controlled eccentric for strength building
L-Sit Pull-Up: Legs held in front for added core challenge
Commando Pull-Up: Alternating side-to-side neutral grip
Archer Pull-Up: One arm does most of the work for advanced strength

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lack of Strength: Start with band-assisted or machine-assisted pull-ups
Shoulder Pain: Try neutral grip pull-ups or reduce range of motion
Elbow Pain: Check grip width, try chin-ups or neutral grip
Grip Weakness: Use chalk or straps, practice dead hangs
No Pull-Up Bar: Use a sturdy door frame, tree branch, or playground equipment
Overweight: Use band assistance or lat pulldowns to build baseline strength
Learning Stage: Start with dead hangs, then work on negatives (slow lowering)
